n: Joash became king at seven and reigned forty years (about 835–796 BC). His mother Zibiah was from Beersheba.
Joash did right as long as Jehoiada the priest lived. His faithfulness depended on his mentor — a warning about borrowed faith.

f.w: all the days of Jehoiada the priest

n: Jehoiada arranged two marriages for Joash, and he had children — rebuilding the nearly extinct royal line of David.
Joash, who had grown up hidden in the temple, set his heart on repairing it.
He told the priests and Levites to collect money yearly from all Israel for the repairs and to do it quickly — but the Levites delayed.
Joash confronted Jehoiada: why haven’t you required the Levites to collect the tax Moses commanded for the tabernacle?

f.g: The half-shekel offering for the sanctuary.
The tent of the testimony, which housed the covenant tablets.

n: The repairs were urgent because Athaliah’s sons had broken into the temple and used its holy things to worship the Baals.

f.g: The only time Chronicles uses such a direct label for a person.

n: So the king had a chest made and placed outside the temple gate — a public collection box.
A proclamation went out throughout Judah to bring the offering Moses had required in the wilderness.
Leaders and people gave joyfully, filling the chest until the need was met. Willing, joyful giving echoes the offerings for the tabernacle and David’s temple.
When the chest filled, the king’s secretary and the high priest’s officer emptied it and returned it. They collected large amounts this way, with careful accountability.
The king and Jehoiada paid stonemasons, carpenters, and ironworkers to restore the temple.
The workers labored faithfully until the temple was restored to its original condition and strengthened.

f.g: To its proper condition; according to its design.

n: Leftover money was used to make gold and silver vessels for temple worship, and regular burnt offerings continued throughout Jehoiada’s lifetime.
Jehoiada lived to the great age of 130 — a sign in scripture of God’s favor on a righteous life.
Jehoiada was honored with burial among the kings — a priest buried as royalty — because of the good he did for God, His house, and Israel.
After Jehoiada’s death, Judah’s officials came, bowed to Joash with flattery, and he listened to them. Without his mentor, he followed new voices.

f.g: Bowed down in honor — perhaps flattery to win the king’s favor.

n: They abandoned the temple and worshipped Asherah poles and idols, and God’s anger came on Judah and Jerusalem. The temple Joash repaired was now forsaken.
Still, God sent prophets to bring them back. The prophets warned them, but they refused to listen. God’s patience is shown in repeated warnings.
The Spirit came upon Zechariah, Jehoiada’s son, who stood above the people and asked: why break God’s commandments, so you can’t prosper? Because you left the Lord, He has left you.

f.w: because ye have forsaken the LORD, he hath also forsaken you

n: They plotted against him and, at the king’s command, stoned him in the temple courtyard. Jesus later referred to this murder as among the last martyrdoms recorded in the Hebrew Bible.
Joash forgot the kindness of Jehoiada, who had saved his life and crown, and killed his son. Zechariah’s dying words: “May the Lord see and avenge.”

f.w: The LORD look upon it, and require it
f.g: May God see this and call the guilty to account.

n: Within a year, a Syrian army invaded Judah and Jerusalem, killed the officials who had led the people astray, and sent the plunder to Damascus.

f.g: The same leaders who had turned Joash to idolatry (v.17).

n: Though the Syrian force was small, God gave Judah’s huge army into their hands because Judah had forsaken Him. They carried out judgment on Joash.
Wounded and sick, Joash was murdered in his bed by his own officials as revenge for killing Jehoiada’s son. He was buried in Jerusalem but not in the royal tombs where Jehoiada lay.

f.g: The plural may emphasize the crime, or include other sons.

n: The conspirators were Zabad and Jehozabad, sons of Ammonite and Moabite mothers. The Chronicler notes their foreign mothers, perhaps echoing the idolatry Joash embraced.
Further details about Joash’s sons, the prophecies against him, and the temple repairs were in the commentary on the book of the kings. His son Amaziah succeeded him.

f.w: the story of the book of the kings
f.g: Hebrew midrash — an explanatory account or commentary.
